title: CTS Practical Theology — Unit 10: Finishing Well — Dry Seasons and Perseverance

blocks.en: 🌱 Practical Theology — Unit 10: Finishing Well — Dry Seasons and Perseverance
blocks.es_reference: 🌱 Teología Práctica — Unidad 10: Terminar Bien — Tiempos de Sequía y la Perseverancia

blocks.en: Professors: Dr. Wayne Cook & Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesores: Dr. Wayne Cook y Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: Introduction
blocks.es_reference: Introducción

blocks.en: Every believer meets dry seasons — stretches of the road when God seems silent and still. We pray and hear nothing; we wait and nothing seems to change. Finishing well means trusting God through those seasons all the way to the end. The Scriptures do not hide these moments; they show that even the faithful sometimes hear no voice and see no visible action from God — and that those seasons have a purpose. The great truth of this unit is simple: God's silence is not absence, and God's stillness is not inactivity.
blocks.es_reference: Todo creyente encuentra tiempos de sequía — tramos del camino en que Dios parece callado y quieto. Oramos y no oímos nada; esperamos y nada parece cambiar. Terminar bien significa confiar en Dios a través de esos tiempos hasta el final mismo. Las Escrituras no esconden estos momentos; muestran que aun los fieles a veces no oyen voz alguna ni ven acción visible de Dios — y que esos tiempos tienen un propósito. La gran verdad de esta unidad es sencilla: el silencio de Dios no es ausencia, y la quietud de Dios no es inactividad.

blocks.en: I. The Dry Seasons Are Real
blocks.es_reference: I. Los Tiempos de Sequía Son Reales

blocks.en: Even faithful people walk through valleys where God seems far away. For Israel there were roughly four centuries, between the prophet Malachi and the coming of Christ, without a new prophetic word recognized as Scripture — the period conventionally called the "four hundred silent years," though the years themselves were far from historically empty, filled with real upheaval, literature, and the developments that shaped the world Jesus was born into. Many must have wondered whether God had forgotten them. He had not; He was preparing the world for His Son. The psalmist cried, "How long, O Lord? Will You forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1, NKJV). Elijah, fresh from his great victory on Mount Carmel, collapsed in despair under a juniper tree (1 Kings 19). These dry seasons are not proof that God has left us; they are part of the journey of faith. Silence is not absence, and stillness is not inactivity.
blocks.es_reference: Aun las personas fieles caminan por valles donde Dios parece lejano. Para Israel hubo aproximadamente cuatro siglos entre el profeta Malaquías y la venida de Cristo sin una nueva palabra profética reconocida como Escritura — el período llamado convencionalmente los "cuatrocientos años de silencio," aunque esos años en sí mismos estuvieron lejos de ser históricamente vacíos, llenos de agitación real, literatura, y los sucesos que formaron el mundo en que nació Jesús. Muchos habrán pensado si acaso Dios los había olvidado. No los había olvidado; estaba preparando al mundo para su Hijo. El salmista clamó: "¿Hasta cuándo, oh Jehová? ¿Me olvidarás para siempre?" (Salmo 13:1, RVG). Elías, recién salido de su gran victoria en el monte Carmelo, se derrumbó en desesperación bajo un enebro (1 Reyes 19). Estos tiempos de sequía no prueban que Dios nos haya dejado; son parte del camino de la fe. El silencio no es ausencia, y la quietud no es inactividad.

blocks.en: II. When God Seems Silent
blocks.es_reference: II. Cuando Dios Parece Callado

blocks.en: When heaven seems quiet, remember first that God has already spoken. "God, who at various times and in various ways spoke in time past to the fathers by the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by His Son" (Hebrews 1:1–2, NKJV). We often crave a fresh word when the foundational word — His Word in Scripture, and supremely in Christ — has already been given. Sometimes His silence is simply beyond us: God answered Job not with explanations but with questions, "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" (Job 38:4, NKJV). And God often speaks softly — not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but in "a still small voice" (1 Kings 19:12, NKJV). So He says, "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:10, NKJV). Silence also matures our faith, "for without faith it is impossible to please Him" (Hebrews 11:6, NKJV); if every prayer were answered with thunder, there would be no room left for faith.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando el cielo parece quedar en silencio, recuerde primero que Dios ya ha hablado. "Dios, habiendo hablado muchas veces y de muchas maneras en otro tiempo a los padres por los profetas, en estos postreros días nos ha hablado por su Hijo" (Hebreos 1:1–2, RVG). A menudo ansiamos una palabra nueva cuando la palabra fundamental — su Palabra en la Escritura, y supremamente en Cristo — ya ha sido dada. A veces su silencio sencillamente nos sobrepasa: Dios respondió a Job no con explicaciones, sino con preguntas: "¿Dónde estabas cuando yo fundaba la tierra?" (Job 38:4, RVG). Y Dios habla muchas veces en voz baja — no en el viento, ni en el terremoto, ni en el fuego, sino en "un silbo apacible y delicado" (1 Reyes 19:12, RVG). Por eso dice: "Estad quietos, y conoced que yo soy Dios" (Salmo 46:10, RVG). El silencio también hace madurar nuestra fe, "porque sin fe es imposible agradar a Dios" (Hebreos 11:6, RVG); si cada oración fuese respondida con truenos, no quedaría lugar para la fe.

blocks.en: III. When God Seems Still
blocks.es_reference: III. Cuando Dios Parece Quieto

blocks.en: Sometimes God speaks but does not act — at least not yet. When Lazarus was sick, "Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when He heard that he was sick, He stayed two more days in the place where He was" (John 11:5–6, NKJV). The delay was not indifference; it set the stage for resurrection. Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to be removed, and the Lord answered, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9, NKJV). Even our Lord prayed in Gethsemane, "not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew 26:39, NKJV). God's apparent stillness is never idleness; while we wait, He is preparing both the answer and our hearts. "Therefore the Lord will wait, that He may be gracious to you... Blessed are all those who wait for Him" (Isaiah 30:18, NKJV).
blocks.es_reference: A veces Dios habla pero no actúa — al menos no todavía. Cuando Lázaro estaba enfermo, "amaba Jesús a Marta, y a su hermana, y a Lázaro. Cuando oyó, pues, que estaba enfermo, se quedó aún dos días en el lugar donde estaba" (Juan 11:5–6, RVG). La demora no era indiferencia; preparó el escenario para la resurrección. Pablo rogó tres veces que su aguijón fuese quitado, y el Señor respondió: "Bástate mi gracia; porque mi poder se perfecciona en la debilidad" (2 Corintios 12:9, RVG). Aun nuestro Señor oró en Getsemaní: "no sea como yo quiero, sino como tú" (Mateo 26:39, RVG). La aparente quietud de Dios nunca es ociosidad; mientras esperamos, Él prepara tanto la respuesta como nuestro corazón. "Por tanto, Jehová esperará para tener piedad de vosotros... bienaventurados todos los que le esperan" (Isaías 30:18, RVG).

blocks.en: IV. Perseverance: Running to the Finish
blocks.es_reference: IV. La Perseverancia: Correr hasta la Meta

blocks.en: Because the road has dry stretches, the Christian life calls for endurance. "Let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith" (Hebrews 12:1–2, NKJV). The testing of our faith is not wasted: "the testing of your faith produces patience... that you may be perfect and complete, lacking nothing" (James 1:3–4, NKJV). And so we are told, "let us not grow weary while doing good, for in due season we shall reap if we do not lose heart" (Galatians 6:9, NKJV). Perseverance is not a way of earning God's favor; it is leaning on His sustaining grace one step at a time.
blocks.es_reference: Porque el camino tiene tramos secos, la vida cristiana exige perseverancia. "Corramos con paciencia la carrera que tenemos por delante, puestos los ojos en Jesús, el autor y consumador de la fe" (Hebreos 12:1–2, RVG). La prueba de nuestra fe no es en vano: "la prueba de vuestra fe produce paciencia... para que seáis perfectos y cabales, sin que os falte cosa alguna" (Santiago 1:3–4, RVG). Por eso se nos dice: "no nos cansemos, pues, de hacer bien; porque a su tiempo segaremos, si no desmayamos" (Gálatas 6:9, RVG). La perseverancia no es un medio para ganar el favor de Dios; es apoyarse en su gracia sustentadora un paso a la vez.

blocks.en: V. Finishing Well
blocks.es_reference: V. Terminar Bien

blocks.en: The goal is not merely to begin but to finish. At the end of his life Paul could say, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Finally, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness" (2 Timothy 4:7–8, NKJV). Yet our confidence to finish is not in our own strength to endure but in God's faithfulness to complete what He began: "He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6, NKJV). The same grace that saved us will keep us to the end. We who belong to Christ are held fast by Him — and that is why we can pass through the silent and the still seasons without losing heart.
blocks.es_reference: La meta no es solo comenzar, sino terminar. Al final de su vida Pablo pudo decir: "He peleado la buena batalla, he acabado la carrera, he guardado la fe. Por lo demás, me está reservada la corona de justicia" (2 Timoteo 4:7–8, RVG). Sin embargo, nuestra confianza para terminar no está en nuestras propias fuerzas para perseverar, sino en la fidelidad de Dios para completar lo que comenzó: "el que comenzó en vosotros la buena obra, la perfeccionará hasta el día de Jesucristo" (Filipenses 1:6, RVG). La misma gracia que nos salvó nos guardará hasta el fin. Los que somos de Cristo somos sostenidos firmemente por Él — y por eso podemos pasar por los tiempos callados y quietos sin desmayar.

blocks.en: Conclusion
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión

blocks.en: When God seems silent, trust the Word He has already spoken. When God seems still, trust His timing and His sufficient grace. He has not forgotten you; behind the silence and the stillness is a God who sees, who cares, and who is always working — even when we cannot see it. Lift your eyes to Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith, and run on. The One who began the good work in you will surely complete it. So do not lose heart — finish well.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Dios parezca callado, confíe en la Palabra que ya ha hablado. Cuando Dios parezca quieto, confíe en su tiempo y en su gracia suficiente. Él no lo ha olvidado; detrás del silencio y la quietud hay un Dios que ve, que se preocupa y que siempre obra — aun cuando no podemos verlo. Ponga los ojos en Jesús, el autor y consumador de su fe, y siga corriendo. El que comenzó en usted la buena obra ciertamente la completará. Así que no desmaye — termine bien.

mc.stem: What does this unit mean by 'dry seasons'?
options: A sure sign that a person was never truly saved
Times when God has abandoned the believer forever
Times when God seems silent and still, which even faithful believers experience
Periods that only unbelievers go through

mc.stem: What were the 'four hundred silent years'?
options: The years between Malachi and the coming of Christ, without a new prophetic word recognized as Scripture - yet God was preparing the world for His Son
A time when God had truly forgotten Israel
A period invented by later writers
The years of Israel's wilderness wandering

mc.stem: According to Hebrews 1:1-2, how has God spoken in these last days?
options: Only through dreams
Only through the law of Moses
He no longer speaks at all
By His Son - so we often seek a fresh word when the foundational word is already given

mc.stem: How did God answer Job out of the whirlwind (Job 38)?
options: With a detailed explanation of his suffering
Not with explanations but with questions, such as 'Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?'
With silence and nothing more
By restoring everything at once

mc.stem: In 1 Kings 19, God came to Elijah not in wind, earthquake, or fire, but in:
options: A burning bush
A loud trumpet blast
A still small voice
A pillar of cloud

mc.stem: What does Psalm 46:10 tell us to do?
options: 'Be still, and know that I am God'
Work harder to earn God's answer
Demand an immediate reply
Stop praying altogether

mc.stem: Why does the unit say God's silence can mature our faith (Hebrews 11:6)?
options: Because faith is unimportant to God
Because 'without faith it is impossible to please Him'; if every prayer were answered with thunder, there would be no room for faith
Because God enjoys leaving us in the dark
Because faith only mattered in the Old Testament

mc.stem: Why did Jesus stay two more days when He heard Lazarus was sick (John 11:5-6)?
options: Because He did not care about the family
Because He was too far away to come
Because He had forgotten His promise
Not from indifference, but to set the stage for resurrection - His delay was divine design

mc.stem: What was the Lord's answer to Paul's plea about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:9)?
options: 'You have asked wrongly'
'I will remove it at once'
'My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness'
God gave no answer at all

mc.stem: What did Jesus pray in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39)?
options: That He might avoid the cross entirely
'Not as I will, but as You will'
That the disciples would stay awake
That God would send angels to fight

mc.stem: What does Isaiah 30:18 say the Lord does while we wait?
options: He waits to be gracious to us, and blessed are all who wait for Him
He turns away from us
He grows impatient with us
He cancels His promises

mc.stem: According to the unit, God's apparent stillness is:
options: Proof that He is powerless
A sign He has changed His mind
A reason to give up
Never idleness - while we wait, He is preparing both the answer and our hearts

mc.stem: What does Hebrews 12:1-2 tell us to do as we run the race?
options: Stop running when the road is hard
Run as fast as possible in our own strength
Run with endurance, looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith
Run only when we feel God's presence

mc.stem: What does James 1:3-4 say the testing of our faith produces?
options: Bitterness and doubt
Patience, so that we may be perfect and complete, lacking nothing
A reason to quit
Nothing of value

mc.stem: What does Galatians 6:9 promise?
options: That doing good is pointless
That we will reap immediately
That only the strong will be rewarded
That in due season we shall reap if we do not lose heart, so let us not grow weary in doing good

mc.stem: How does the unit describe perseverance?
options: Not earning God's favor, but leaning on His sustaining grace one step at a time
Something only super-Christians can do
Proof that we save ourselves
A way to earn God's favor by our endurance

mc.stem: What could Paul say at the end of his life (2 Timothy 4:7-8)?
options: That he had earned heaven by his own strength
That he had failed and given up
That the race was not worth running
'I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith,' with a crown of righteousness laid up for him

mc.stem: On what is the believer's confidence to finish well finally based (Philippians 1:6)?
options: On God's faithfulness - He who began a good work in us will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ
On our own willpower to endure
On never facing any hardship
On the strength of other believers alone

mc.stem: How does this unit connect finishing well to the grace of salvation?
options: It says grace gets us started but we must finish on our own
It says the same grace that saved us will keep us to the end, so we are held fast by Christ
It says perseverance replaces grace
It says only some believers will be kept

mc.stem: What is the unit's closing encouragement?
options: Give up when God seems silent
Demand that God act on our schedule
Trust the Word God has spoken and His sufficient grace; lift your eyes to Jesus and run on, for He who began the good work will finish it
Trust only what we can see

sa.prompt: What does this unit mean by 'dry seasons,' and who experiences them?
sa.model: 'Dry seasons' are stretches of the Christian life when God seems silent and still — we pray and hear nothing, we wait and nothing seems to change. Every believer experiences them; the unit shows that even the faithful, like the psalmist and Elijah, walk through valleys where God seems far away.

sa.prompt: What were the four hundred silent years, and what was God doing?
sa.model: The "four hundred silent years" is the conventional name for the period between the prophet Malachi and the coming of Christ, without a new prophetic word recognized as Scripture -- though the years themselves were historically eventful, not empty. Though it seemed God had forgotten His people, He was actually preparing the world for the coming of His Son.

sa.prompt: According to Hebrews 1:1-2, how has God already spoken?
sa.model: Hebrews 1:1-2 says that God, who spoke in time past to the fathers by the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by His Son. God has already spoken supremely and finally through Christ and through His written Word, so we already possess His foundational word even when we crave a fresh one.

sa.prompt: When God seems silent, what reasons does this unit give?
sa.model: When God seems silent, this unit gives several reasons: God has already spoken through Christ and Scripture; sometimes His silence is simply beyond our understanding, as with Job; God often speaks softly in a still small voice rather than dramatic signs; and silence matures our faith, since faith requires room to trust without constant confirmation.

sa.prompt: What do 1 Kings 19:12 and Psalm 46:10 teach about how God speaks and our response?
sa.model: 1 Kings 19:12 shows that God spoke to Elijah not in the wind, earthquake, or fire, but in a still small voice, and Psalm 46:10 says, 'Be still, and know that I am God.' Together they teach that God often speaks gently rather than dramatically, and our response should be to quiet ourselves and listen rather than demanding loud, visible signs.

sa.prompt: When God seems still, what do John 11 and 2 Corinthians 12:9 show us?
sa.model: John 11 shows that when Jesus heard Lazarus was sick, He stayed two more days rather than rushing to heal him — the delay was not indifference but set the stage for resurrection. 2 Corinthians 12:9 shows Paul's plea for his thorn to be removed answered not with removal but with 'My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness' — together they teach that God's apparent stillness is never idleness but purposeful preparation.

sa.prompt: How does Hebrews 12:1-2 describe running the Christian race?
sa.model: Hebrews 12:1-2 describes running the Christian race with endurance, laying aside every weight and sin, and looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith. It pictures the Christian life as a long-distance race requiring patient endurance, with our eyes fixed on Christ rather than on the difficulty of the course itself.

sa.prompt: What does the unit say perseverance is, and what it is not?
sa.model: The unit says perseverance is leaning on God's sustaining grace one step at a time through the dry stretches of the road. It is NOT a way of earning God's favor — endurance does not purchase acceptance with God but simply walks out, step by step, the grace already given.

sa.prompt: On what is our confidence to finish well based? Use Philippians 1:6 or 2 Timothy 4:7-8.
sa.model: Our confidence to finish well is based not on our own strength to endure but on God's faithfulness, as Philippians 1:6 says: 'He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.' The same grace that saved us is the grace that keeps us to the end, so our finishing depends on His faithfulness, not merely our willpower.

sa.prompt: What is the unit's closing encouragement when God seems silent or still?
sa.model: The unit's closing encouragement is: when God seems silent, trust the Word He has already spoken; when God seems still, trust His timing and sufficient grace. He has not forgotten us, and we are urged to lift our eyes to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith, and run on without losing heart, trusting Him to finish the good work He began.
